app.title: Fire Calendar: Central Highlands & Northwest Vietnam
app.subtitle: 25 years of NASA satellite hotspot detections, harmonized across MODIS and VIIRS into one consistent record.

anomaly.title: Compared with a typical year
anomaly.explanation: "Normal" is the middle half of all values recorded for the same month, province and land cover from 2003 to 2025. Months above that range are flagged as above normal.

sections.heading: Why this tool
sections.body: Every dry season, the Central Highlands and Northwest Vietnam see many forest fires and agricultural burns. Remote, hilly terrain slows detection and response, so knowing when and where burning usually peaks helps forest rangers plan patrols and resources.

sections.heading: What the data is
sections.body: NASA satellites detect hotspots: image pixels that are unusually hot, usually because of burning. MODIS has recorded hotspots since 2000; VIIRS, a newer and more detailed sensor, since 2012.

sections.heading: How we harmonized the record
sections.body: VIIRS detects many more hotspots than MODIS over the same area. Using 2012–2026, when both sensors operated, we learned how MODIS counts translate into VIIRS counts, separately for forest and agricultural land, and converted the whole record to one VIIRS-equivalent scale.

sections.heading: How the patrol priority map works
sections.body: For each 1 km square we counted in how many years (2012–2025) VIIRS detected at least one hotspot in a given month. We then estimated ground access from the distance to the nearest vehicle road in OpenStreetMap and the mean terrain slope from NASADEM. Places that burn often and are hard to reach are marked high priority, so rangers can position people and equipment there before the peak month.

data_sources.name: VIIRS 375 m Active Fire, Collection 2
data_sources.period: S-NPP Jan 2012 – Nov 2026; NOAA-20 Apr 2018 – present; NOAA-21 Mar 2023 – present

limitations: Satellites cannot see through clouds, so hotspots in cloudy months are undercounted.
A hotspot is a hot pixel, not a single fire: one large fire can produce many hotspots.
Land cover comes from a 500 m global map and may misclassify some local forest types.
Access is an estimate: OpenStreetMap often misses forest tracks and farm roads, so some places marked moderate may be easier to reach in reality.

patrol.title: Patrol priority map
patrol.subtitle: Where hotspots recur in the selected month, and how hard those places are to reach.
patrol.popup: Hotspots in {years} of 14 years ({month_name}, 2012–2025). Access: {access}. Nearest vehicle road ≈ {dist_km} km (estimate). Mean slope {slope}°.
patrol.popup_unknown: Hotspots in {years} of 14 years ({month_name}, 2012–2025). Access: not assessed.
patrol.explanation: Each square is about 1 km. Priority is high when hotspots appeared in at least half of the years 2012–2025 for this month and the place is hard to reach: steep terrain, or far from vehicle roads on moderately steep ground. Access uses OpenStreetMap roads and NASADEM slope, so it is an estimate.
